    Kinematics of Rigid Bodies

    Rigid-body kinematics involves linear and angular displacements, velocities and accelerations.

    #Rotation

    For rotation with constant angular acceleration,

    💡
    ω=ω0​+αt
    💡
    θ=θ0​+ω0​t+21​αt2
    💡
    ω2=ω0​2+2a(θ−θ0​)

    v=r˙

    v=ω×r

    a=v˙

    a=ω×r˙+ω˙×r

    a=ω×v+α×r

    💡
    v=ω×r
    💡
    at​=α×r
    💡
    an​=ω×v
    💡
    v=rω
    💡
    at​=rα

    #Absolute Motion

    In absolute-motion analysis to describe the kinematics of rigid bodies, it involves both linear and angular variables. If the angular variables are specified by a anticlockwise angle θ, an anticlockwise motion will be considered positive and vice versa.

    #Motion Relative to Fixed Axes

    #Relative Velocity Due to Rotation

    A rigid body moves in the plane of the figure from position AB to A′B′.

    The movement can be split into two parts — a displacement followed by a rotation. First, the body translates to the parallel position A′′B′ with the displacement ΔrB​. Then, the body rotates about B′ through an angle Δθ. This rotation results in A′′ rotating to A′
    with displacement ΔrA/B​ of A with respect to B.

    With B as the reference point for the rotation, the total displacement and velocity is,

    ΔrA​=ΔrB​+ΔrA/B​

    vA​=vB​+vA/B​

    Relative displacement ΔrA/B​ has magnitude rΔθ. Thus, the magnitude of vA/B​ is rω.

    💡
    vA/B​=ω×r
    💡
    vA​=vB​+ω×rA/B​

    The relative velocity component represents the effect of circular motion about B and thus, is always perpendicular to the line joining the two points.

    #Instantaneous Center of Zero Velocity

    Instead of adding the relative velocity due to rotation about a convenient reference
    point to the velocity of the reference point, we now choose a unique reference point
    which momentarily has zero velocity.

    Thus, the rigid body is considered to be in pure rotation about an axis, normal to the
    plane of motion, passing through this point. The axis is called the instantaneous axis
    of zero velocity, and the intersection of this axis with the plane of motion is the instantaneous center of zero velocity.

    Although the instantaneous center of zero velocity is momentarily at rest, its acceleration
    is generally not zero. Thus, this point may not be used as an instantaneous center of zero acceleration.

    #Example 1

    The point on the rim of the wheel in contact
    with the ground has no velocity if the wheel
    is not slipping. Thus, it is the instantaneous
    center of zero velocity.

    ω=0.33​=10 rad/s

    #Relative Acceleration Due to Rotation

    Motion of a rigid body can be split into translational and rotational motion — vA​=vB​+vA/B​.

    Since relative motion is circular, relative-acceleration term will have a normal component directed from A to B and a tangential component.

    💡
    aA​=aB​+aA/Bt​​+aA/Bn​​
    💡
    aA​=aB​+α×rA/B​−ω2(rA/B​)
    💡
    aA​=aB​+α×rA/B​+ω×(ω×rA/B​)

    #Example 1

    aA​=aO​+aA/On​​+aA/Ot​​

    aO​=aO​cosθi+aO​sinθj

    aA/On​​=r0​ω2=r0​(rvO​​)2

    aA/Ot​​=r0​α=r0​(raO​​)

    Resolving aO​ in the n- and t-directions,

    aOn​​=aO​cosθ

    aOt​​=aO​sinθ

    Summing the vectors in the directions,

    aAn​​=aO​cosθ+r0​ω2

    aAt​​=aO​sinθ+r0​α

    aA​=(aAn​​)2+(aAt​​)2​

    aA/Bn​​=−76​k×[−76​k×(−175i+50j)]

    aA/Bn​​=(76​)2(175i−50j) mm/s2

    #Motion Relative to Rotating Axes

    Consider the plane motion of particles A and B
    in the fixed X-Y plane. We observe the motion
    of A from a moving reference frame x-y which
    has its origin attached to B and rotates with an angular velocity ω=ωk.

    The absolute position vector of A is,

    rA​=rB​+r=rB​+(xi+yj)

    Unit vectors i and j rotates with the x-y axes.

    di=dθj

    dtdi​=dtdθ​j

    i˙=ωj

    dj=dθ(−i)

    dtdj​=dtdθ​(−i)

    j˙​=−ωi

    💡
    i˙=ω×i
    💡
    j˙​=ω×j

    #Relative Velocity

    Taking the dt of the position vector,

    dtd​rA​=dtd​rB​+dtd​r

    dtd​rA​=dtd​rB​+dtd​(xi+yj)

    vA​=vB​+(xi˙+yj˙​)+(x˙i+y˙​j)

    The second term can be written as,

    xi˙+yj˙​=ω×xi+ω×yj

    xi˙+yj˙​=ω×(xi+yj)

    xi˙+yj˙​=ω×r

    💡
    vA​=vB​+ω×r+vrel​
    💡
    vA​=vB​+ω×rA/B​+(vA/B​)xy​

    The term vrel​ is velocity relative to the x-y frame of reference. ω×r is the difference between the relative velocities as measured from non-rotating and rotating axes.

    #Relative Acceleration

    Taking the time derivative of the relative-velocity equation,

    dtd​vA​=dtd​vB​+dtd​(ω×r)+dtd​vrel​

    aA​=aB​+(ω˙×r+ω×r˙)+v˙rel​

    From the derivation of the relative-velocity equation,

    dtd​r=dtd​(xi+yj)

    r˙=ω×r+vrel​

    The third term can be written as,

    ω×r˙=ω×(ω×r+vrel​)

    ω×r˙=ω×(ω×r)+ω×vrel​

    The last term can be written as,

    v˙rel​=dtd​(x˙i+y˙​j)

    v˙rel​=(x˙i˙+y˙​j˙​)+(x¨i+y¨​j)

    v˙rel​=ω×vrel​+arel​

    💡
    aA​=aB​+ω˙×r+ω×(ω×r)+2ω×vrel​+arel​
    💡
    aA​=aB​+ω˙×rA/B​+ω×(ω×rA/B​)+2ω×(vA/B​)xy​+(aA/B​)xy​

    The term arel​ is acceleration relative to the x-y frame of reference. The terms ω˙×r
    and     ω×(ω×r) are the tangential and normal components of acceleration aP/B​
    of coincident point     P in its circular motion with respect to B.

    • Magnitude of ∣arelt​​∣=s¨=a
    • Magnitude of ∣ω˙×r∣=rθ¨=rα
    • Magnitude of ∣ω×(ω×r)∣=rω2

    #Coriolis Acceleration

    The term 2ω×vrel​ is called the Coriolis acceleration — the difference between the acceleration of A relative to P as measured from non-rotating and rotating axes. Its direction is always normal to vrel​.

    Consider a rotating disk with a radial slot in which particle A is confined to slide. The disk turns with
    a constant angular velocity ω. The particle moves along the slot with a constant speed vrel​ relative
    to the slot.

    Velocity components of A:

    • Velocity x˙ due to motion along the slot
    • Velocity xω due to rotation of the slot

    Change in velocity of A:

    • Due to change in direction of vrel​ — x˙ dθ
    • Due to change in magnitude of xω — ω dx
    • Due to change in direction of xω — xω dθ

    Dividing each velocity component by dt, we get x˙ dtdθ​=x˙ω and ω dtdx​=ωx˙.

    Summing up the acceleration component, we get x˙ω+ωx˙=2ωx˙=2ωv.

    The term 2ωv is the magnitude of the Coriolis acceleration 2ω×vrel​.

    Dividing the remaining velocity component by dt, we get xω dtdθ​=xω2.

    The term xω2 is the normal component of acceleration with respect to B.

    For this example, with the origin B taken as the fixed center O, aB​=0. With constant angular velocity, ω˙×r=0 and with vrel​ constant in magnitude and no curvature to
    the slot,     arel​=0. Thus, acceleration of A becomes aA​=ω×(ω×r)+2ω×vrel​.
    If the slot in the disk had been curved, there would be a normal component of acceleration relative to the slot such that     arel​=0.

    #Rotating vs Non-Rotating Systems

    Let P be a point coincident with A at the instant under consideration.

    Comparison of relative velocity for rotating and non-rotating reference axes.

    💡
    vA​=vB​+ω×r+vrel​vA​=vB​+vP/B​+vA/P​​vA​=vB​+       vA/B​

    Comparison of relative acceleration for rotating and non-rotating reference axes.

    💡
    aA​=aB​+ω˙×rA/B​+ω×(ω×rA/B​)​+2ω×(vA/B​)xy​+(aA/B​)xy​​aA​=aB​+                    aP/B​                   +                  aA/P​​aA​=aB​+                                              aA/B​

    ω˙×rOA​=−10k×6i

    ω˙×rOA​=−60j in/s2
